sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2611.08924.question: In the QAT experiments, which model sizes and training tasks compare ResQAdam with AdamW, GaLore, and LDAdam, and what are the measured model-quality, optimizer-state memory, and training-throughput results?

passages.text: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .
We compare ResQAdam with AdamW in from-scratch QAT and QAT fine-tuning, in terms of training loss, final perplexity and accuracy, and optimizer-state memory.

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Values in each cell are formatted as AdamW / ResQAdam , with relative changes in parentheses. AdamW / ResQAdam Llama 3.2-1B Qwen2.5-1.5B Qwen3 4B-Base Opt. State Memory (GB) 7.78 / 2.16 ( ↓ \downarrow 72.2%) 10.48 / 3.01( ↓ \downarrow 71.3%) 29.07 / 7.78 ( ↓ \downarrow 73.2%) Total Peak Memory (GB) 33.33 / 28.24 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 43.93 / 37.19 ( ↓ \downarrow 15.3%) 99.14 / 79.77 ( ↓ \downarrow 19.5%) Throughput (# token/s) 29.36k / 28.94k ( ↓ \downarrow 1.4%) 18.31k / 18.19k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.6%) 9.64k / 9.56k ( ↓ \downarrow 0.8%) To evaluate hardware efficiency, we compare ResQAdam against AdamW in terms of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput. Total peak memory is defined as the maximum GPU memory consumed during training, encompassing weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states. All experiments utilize the Basic QAT framework with a W4A4G128 quantization configuration and a context length of 4096. Training is conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. The micro-batch size is set to 1 with 128 gradient accumulation steps. ResQAdam uses a uniform projection rank of r = 64 r=64 . The reported optimizer-state memory strictly accounts for the transformer backbone and excludes the embedding and language modeling head layers.

As detailed in Table 3 , ResQAdam consistently reduces the optimizer state footprint by over 71% across 3 different LLMs. This efficiency directly translates to a 15.3% to 19.5% reduction in total peak memory. This substantial memory reduction incurs minimal computational overhead. The training throughput decreases by less than 2% compared to standard AdamW in all evaluated cases. These results show that our amortized update strategy substantially alleviates the optimizer-state memory bottleneck of QAT while maintaining competitive training throughput.

Table 4: Perplexity comparison of memory-efficient optimizers under diverse QAT paradigms and quantization configurations. Projection-based optimizers use rank 64. Structural factorization methods such as AdaFactor ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) keep the full parameter dimensionality but approximate the second moment by row and column statistics. Table 4 reports the average perplexity on WikiText-2 and C4. In from-scratch QAT, every baseline is far behind ResQAdam in both quantization settings, by a margin much larger than the differences we observe between ResQAdam and AdamW in Table 1 . This is consistent with our hypothesis that confining the update to a low-rank subspace, or replacing the second moment by a factorized approximation, loses part of the correction that QAT relies on. In fine-tuning the picture depends on the bit width. At W2A16G128 the projection-based methods remain clearly behind, whereas at W4A4G128, where quantization error is small, all optimizers land within a narrow range and the choice of optimizer matters little.

Fine-tuning changes the behavior of a pretrained model by writing an update relative to what that model already knows. How many bits are actually required to preserve this acquired behavior? Parameter count, adapter rank, and numerical precision measure storage, but need not measure the information that matters functionally. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) provides a clean setting for studying this question: the base model remains frozen while the learned update is isolated in a separate adapter that can be compressed after training. We take a receiver-relative rate–distortion view of this process. As illustrated in Figure 1 , fine-tuning acts as an encoder, the adapter as a finite-rate message, and the frozen model as side information available when that message is decoded. We measure rate by the exact serialized size of a compressed adapter and distortion by the behavior of the resulting composed model. For a fixed retention target, the behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} is the smallest measured rate that preserves the required fraction of the held-out fine-tuning gain. Behavioral rate also increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budget. On Qwen2.5-7B, for example, GSM8K accuracy falls from 77.6% to 23.7% after corrupted fine-tuning and returns to 82.9% after compression. Singular-direction analyses show that harmful and useful effects are distributed unevenly across the update, while matched-norm controls show that the recovery is not exactly equivalent to scalar rescaling. Finally, once an update has been trained, its behavioral rate closely tracks how far it can be shrunk before losing its gain. Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning is not an intrinsic property of the data or of parameter displacement alone: it depends on the frozen receiver, the behavior to preserve, and how the learned corrections are represented within the update.

We begin by examining how post-training compression affects fine-tuned behavior. Controlled compression lets us separate numerical reconstruction from functional preservation while keeping both the learned checkpoint and the frozen model fixed. These diagnostics show that ordinary parameter-space fidelity is not sufficient to predict which compressed adapters preserve the behavior acquired during fine-tuning.

We study post-training compression of LoRA adapters across frozen language models from 0.5B to 32B parameters, including Qwen2.5-{0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B}, Qwen3-8B-Base, Mistral-7B-v0.1, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-2-9B. Each adapter is trained once and then compressed over a range of operating points, without retraining. At one bit per value and above, we quantize the LoRA factors row-wise; below one bit, we additionally remove paired rank directions. Each compressed representation, including its decoding metadata, is serialized to disk, reloaded, and evaluated in composition with the frozen model. We report realized file size normalized by the number of scalar values in the uncompressed adapter. Full training configurations, codec details, datasets, and evaluation procedures are given in Appendix A .

The final recovered adapter is rank 1 and one bit, raising the possibility that the same result could be obtained by training a small adapter from the start. We therefore train corrupted adapters at ranks 1, 2, 4, and 16, and compress every checkpoint to the same rank-1, one-bit endpoint. Figure 11 b shows that recovery is substantially stronger when additional rank was available during training: final GSM8K accuracy rises from approximately 60% when trained at rank 1 to approximately 78–81% when trained at ranks 2–16. Compression is therefore not equivalent to directly training the final low-rank representation. Higher training rank appears to make useful behavior more recoverable under the subsequent bottleneck, although these experiments do not establish the mechanism by which this separation emerges. (b) GSM8K accuracy after corrupted adapters trained at different ranks are all compressed to the same rank-1, one-bit endpoint.

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly used in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), often under similar optimizer settings. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks across multiple models show that the respective configurations for SFT and RL yield the best performance among the compared methods in most evaluated settings.

passages.section: Baseline subtraction separates the LoRA dynamics of SFT and RL (Section 2 ).
passages.text: Across various Llama and Qwen models on GSM8K [ 6 ] and MATH [ 9 ] , we observed that RL with verifiable reward via group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [ 33 ] concentrates the spectrum of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} at every learning rate; whereas SFT expands it at moderate learning rates that can facilitate desired downstream performance. For the dynamics of the singular subspaces, we observed that RL with small learning rates rotates the singular subspace much faster than SFT. Moreover, interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we find that both contrasts appear only once a group-mean baseline is subtracted from the reward, pinpointing baseline subtraction as the key mechanism that separates the LoRA dynamics of SFT and RL.

passages.section: Baseline subtraction tilts the balance between coherent fitting and gradient noise (Section 3 ).
passages.text: To understand these contrasts, we analyze a quadratic multi-index model in which a LoRA adapter is trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on pairs of correlated inputs, each pair modeling a GRPO group of responses sampled for the same prompt. Two forces compete in this model: coherent fitting that is linear in the learning rate and concentrates spectral energy on strongly responding directions, as well as feedback from gradient noise that is quadratic in the learning rate and redistributes the spectral energy more evenly. Subtracting a group-mean baseline largely cancels the gradient component shared across a group’s responses, which drives coherent fitting along pretrained directions and anchors successive updates to similar directions, while retaining most of the component that contrasts responses within the group, and damping the gradient noise from task-irrelevant directions. Coherent fitting thus persists through the contrasts while the redistributing feedback loses relative strength, and gradient noise, no longer anchored by the shared component, steers the update directions more, leading to spectral concentration and faster singular subspace rotation during RL. Nevertheless, baseline subtraction can come at a cost for prediction: coherent fitting of the shared component reduces the risk more efficiently than fitting of the contrasts, cancellation of which shrinks the risk reduction from coherent fitting (linear in the learning rate) relative to the cost of gradient noise (quadratic in the learning rate). The risk-favorable learning rate thus remains low, consistent with the common practice in RL.

passages.section: The dynamics inform stage-specific LoRA optimization (Section 4 ).
passages.text: Our analysis further shows which dynamics accompany the risk-favorable learning rate: training without a baseline (as in SFT) expands the spectrum of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} , whereas training with a baseline (as in RL) concentrates the spectrum and rotates the left singular subspace faster. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor the update of LoRA factors to each stage by combining two standard components, a norm-preserving spectral flattening as in Muon [ 14 ] and a per-factor choice between SGD and Adam update directions. However, it remains unclear whether Muon’s advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token–parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training. The Muon optimizer has recently shown strong empirical performance for pretraining LLMs, challenging AdamW’s status as the standard optimizer for minimizing pretraining loss ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) . Prior work has shown that the pretraining optimization choices that minimize pretraining loss do not necessarily yield the best model after fine-tuning ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . What ultimately matters downstream is the learning–forgetting tradeoff : how well a fine-tuned model learns the target task while retaining its pretrained knowledge. Motivated by this, we ask: Does Muon’s pretraining advantage over AdamW extend to the learning–forgetting tradeoff? To answer this question, we measure the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap , which compares the two optimizers on this tradeoff; a negative gap indicates that the Muon pretrained model dominates the AdamW pretrained model after fine-tuning, and a positive gap indicates the reverse. We show that the answer depends on the pretraining data budget, and find that pretraining data scale reverses the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap . At small budgets, Muon achieves lower fine-tuning loss with less forgetting than AdamW and the fine-tuning gap is negative. At larger budgets, this trend reverses: AdamW achieves a better learning–forgetting tradeoff than Muon, and the fine-tuning gap becomes positive.

In Section 3 , we pretrain OLMo-style 30M–600M models ( Groeneveld et al., 2024 ; Team OLMo et al., 2025 ) on 150 150 M to 154 154 B DCLM tokens ( Li et al., 2024 ) , comparing AdamW and Muon, and fine-tune each base model on four datasets while sweeping the fine-tuning optimizer and learning rate, for nearly 600 pretraining runs and 29,000 fine-tuning runs in total. We show that when tuning pretraining hyperparameters for the lowest pretraining loss, Muon consistently achieves lower loss than AdamW. However, with sufficient pretraining data, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning, reversing the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap. This reversal also holds when we disregard pretraining loss, instead sweeping pretraining hyperparameters to obtain the best learning–forgetting tradeoff after fine-tuning. We additionally show that as model size scales, AdamW surpasses Muon at progressively smaller data budgets . In Section 4 , we investigate why the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap reverses as the pretraining data budget grows. Fine-tuning changes the output distribution, so we generalize fine-tuning updates with perturbations to the output distribution and study which optimizer produces base models that are more robust to such perturbations. To quantify sensitivity to output perturbations, we introduce the margin-to-spread ratio (MSR) , a simple metric derived from the model’s output logits that characterizes robustness. For each prediction, the MSR is the difference between the correct logit and the average of the incorrect logits, normalized by the spread of the incorrect logits ( Section 4.1 ): a prediction is more robust when the MSR is larger.

We test whether the budget trend predicted by Section 4.2 also appears in real language models, beyond the assumptions used in our theoretical analysis. Setup. We evaluate the AdamW and Muon models trained in Section 3 , spanning five model sizes, on held-out DCLM text. We compute the MSR at each token position and report the median over correctly predicted positions. At each position, h h and κ \kappa are the mean and standard deviation of the margins between the correct next-token logit and all other vocabulary logits. We use the median to reduce sensitivity to outliers; Section 4.1 instead uses the mean margin divided by the square root of the mean variance. Experimental Result. Figure 5 plots the MSR for the three model sizes with the widest budget ranges, from 30M to 100M. Muon has a larger MSR at small data budgets, while AdamW has a larger MSR at sufficiently large budgets. As the budget grows, the difference between AdamW’s and Muon’s MSRs increases, and the ratio of AdamW’s MSR to Muon’s crosses one. This shift toward AdamW is consistent with the theoretical budget trend and parallels the reversal in relative robustness to fine-tuning observed in Section 3 . inspect:2611.05022.question: What matrix-factorization assumptions establish that finite Newton–Schulz depth changes entrance rank and bypasses the first gradient-flow saddle? Are there experiments on neural-network or language-model training beyond the theoretical example, and what limitations does the paper state?

passages.text: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton–Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton–Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton–Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four. † † shortheadings: Finite-Depth Newton–Schulz Dynamics / Long † † firstpage: 1 † † heading: 2026 1–

We consider a two-layer neural network with quadratic activation and all second-layer weights fixed to one. This model admits an equivalent representation as a positive-semidefinite matrix factorization. Such quadratic networks provide a tractable setting for analyzing nonlinear training dynamics, and have also been studied through gradient flow and spectral gradient methods ( Martin et al., 2024 ; Martin et al., 2026 ; Braun et al., 2026 ) . We study continuous-time optimization dynamics in which K K cubic Newton–Schulz iterations are applied to the normalized factor gradient, and refer to K K as the spectral depth. For the analysis, we use a two-scale Gaussian initialization: one hidden row is initialized at scale ε \varepsilon , while the remaining rows have scale ε b \varepsilon^{b} , where b > 1 b>1 . The gradient normalization includes an additive stabilization proportional to ε \varepsilon . This choice of initialization scales allows us to identify the leading directional dynamics first and then derive the coupled equations governing the weaker components in the remaining independent directions. We compare trajectories on the same task and with the same underlying Gaussian seed as ε \varepsilon tends to zero, while keeping each spectral depth fixed. Removing the row-dependent initialization scales would instead lead to an isotropic Gaussian initialization, for which the competing directions may exhibit different and potentially richer dynamics. The analysis of this regime remains open.

Another question concerns the extent to which small-initialization asymptotics can determine the subsequent training trajectory. Under suitable structural conditions, gradient flow admits a precise description in which the initialization scale can be used to reverse-engineer the full training dynamics, leading also to a characterization of time-dependent implicit regularization ( Berthier, 2023 ) . For finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics, the nonlinear matrix iteration prevents this reconstruction argument from carrying over directly. Although the dynamics can be analyzed in a small neighborhood of the origin, the resulting local description does not by itself determine the trajectory after leaving that neighborhood. This creates two distinct dynamical scales: the entrance dynamics near the origin and the subsequent evolution away from it. Establishing how the entrance dynamics are transmitted to the later trajectory is one of the main results of this paper.

Following the framework of Li et al. (2021) , which characterizes the first nonzero stationary point selected by gradient flow under suitable assumptions, we study the evolution from small initialization through the first stationary point encountered after escape. This allows us to compare the stationary points approached by gradient descent and by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics. Under an additional structural assumption, we establish a sufficient large-depth guarantee: for all sufficiently large spectral depths, the selected Newton–Schulz continuation approaches a first stationary point whose loss is strictly smaller than that of the first stationary point selected by gradient descent. For smaller depths, our results do not provide a general criterion determining whether the trajectory visits or bypasses the gradient-descent stationary point. Moreover, without the additional assumption, the first stationary points reached by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics and gradient descent may have the same loss. Such equal-loss behavior may reveal further dynamical structures, which we leave for future work. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model and pathwise comparison criteria. Sections 3–5 establish the Gaussian entrance law, continuation criteria, and eventual depth guarantee. Section 6 presents an exact empirical task, and Section 7 discusses the scope of the results and open questions. Detailed proofs are given in the appendices.

Subscripts F \mathrm{F} and op \mathrm{op} denote the Frobenius and operator norms, respectively; vector norms are Euclidean. In this paper, we have studied how finitely many iterations of a nonlinear matrix transformation can reshape optimization dynamics. In a quadratic two-layer network, we have characterized the evolution from small-initialization escape near the origin to the first nonzero stationary stage. Our results provide a precise description of how the number of Newton–Schulz iterations controls early rank selection and regulates the subsequent optimization path. Beyond this particular model, the analysis offers a framework combining spectral dynamics with small-initialization techniques, which may help understand certain training phenomena arising in large-scale neural networks, including language models. An immediate open question is whether similar dynamical descriptions can be established for more general models and under weaker assumptions. Of particular interest are networks with nonlinear activations such as ReLU, high-dimensional training regimes, and deeper architectures, where the interaction between spectral updates and feature learning may lead to richer dynamics.

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

CORE achieves the highest answer accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark group, producing new state-of-the-art results. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves both metrics over the stronger baseline, OpenResearcher, for all three agent models. The gains are largest for Qwen3.8-27B, at 6.39 points in accuracy and 7.40 points in recall. On BrowseComp-Wikipedia, CORE keeps its lead across all three agents. With GPT-5.4, it improves both metrics by more than eight points over OpenResearcher. Higher accuracy therefore comes with broader coverage of the annotated relevant documents in both the web and Wikipedia corpora. See some case studies in Appendix C .

BrowseComp-Plus CM requires searching 553 million ClimbMix documents, our largest corpus. CORE again leads in both accuracy and recall for every agent. Its advantage is most pronounced with Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B. CORE outperforms OpenResearcher by 14.03 points. With GPT-5.4, CORE raises accuracy to 68.42%, compared with 56.14% for OpenResearcher and 50.88% for Tongyi DeepResearch. With Qwen3.8-27B, Tongyi DeepResearch is the stronger baseline in accuracy, and CORE still exceeds both baselines in accuracy and recall.

These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

passages.text: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates descent directions from function values alone, which removes the activation storage required by backpropagation and makes it attractive for memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). Existing low-rank ZO methods either parameterize the additive update through Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation, or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank. In this work, we propose to constrain each additive update block to a fixed-rank matrix manifold while keeping the pretrained weights frozen, so the learned update remains rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning. On this geometry, we build a Riemannian ZO gradient estimator that projects a random matrix onto the tangent space, normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch induced by projection, and further propose Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S. We show that the ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation, and ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. Experiments on LLM fine-tuning tasks show that the proposed algorithms are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of domains ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ) . Fine-tuning these models on downstream tasks is crucial for their practical deployment. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) have emerged as a practical solution, training low-rank updates while keeping pretrained weights frozen ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Hayou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024a ) . However, first-order optimization still incurs substantial memory overhead from storing activations for backpropagation, especially in long-context settings where activations dominate memory. To enhance memory efficiency, zeroth-order (ZO) fine-tuning methods ( Malladi et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) estimate descent directions from function values without backpropagated gradients, avoiding the activation storage required by backward passes ( Spall, 1992 ) .

Recent low-rank ZO fine-tuning methods combine these two directions by restricting the finite-difference search through low-rank perturbations, adapter factors, gradient estimators, or random subspaces ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Song and Li, 2026 ) . Factor-based approaches constrain the learned update through adapter coordinates, whereas low-rank perturbation methods constrain individual ZO steps. These two branches of methods differ in the way of constructing low-rank additive update matrices when optimizing a fixed-rank update matrix. Factor-based adaptation uses a factorized update Δ ​ 𝑾 = 𝑩 ​ 𝑨 \Delta\boldsymbol{W}=\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{A} and optimizes over ( 𝑩 , 𝑨 ) (\boldsymbol{B},\boldsymbol{A}) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . This representation is nonunique, since ( 𝑩 ​ 𝑸 ) ​ ( 𝑸 − 1 ​ 𝑨 ) (\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{Q})(\boldsymbol{Q}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}) gives the same update for any invertible 𝑸 \boldsymbol{Q} . Low-rank perturbation and random-subspace methods instead use restricted finite-difference directions or estimators to construct each ZO step ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024b ) . For example, low-rank perturbation methods form each step from a sampled rank- r r direction 𝑼 ​ 𝑽 ⊤ \boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{V}^{\top} , while random-subspace variants restrict the step direction to a prescribed low-dimensional subspace ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . Although existing low-precision compression methods can effectively reduce communication costs, further reducing the communication footprint to ultra-low-bit formats such as FP4 introduces new challenges, including limited numerical range, sub-byte storage overhead, and increased computational cost from fine-grained quantization. In this paper, we present \textbf{FP4Quant}, a micro-grouped FP4 compression framework for efficient model-parallel LLM training. FP4Quant integrates a micro-grouped dual-scale FP4 quantization mechanism to preserve local tensor distribution characteristics, a warp-cooperative FP4 packing scheme to enable efficient sub-byte data representation, and a hybrid two-level FWHT pipeline to mitigate quantization errors with GPU-aware execution optimization. Experiments on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with Qwen-7B demonstrate up to 1.56$\times$ end-to-end throughput improvement over BF16, revealing a trade-off between throughput and model quality.

candidates.title: LIRA: A More Interpretable Dynamic Loss-Informed Rank Allocation for Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large pretrained models. However, standard LoRA typically assigns a fixed rank profile despite layer- and stage-dependent adaptation needs, while recent adaptive-rank variants often rely on heuristic or first-order signals that provide only an indirect link between rank reallocation and local loss behavior. This leaves the rationale behind each rank reallocation insufficiently interpretable. Motivated by this gap, we propose LIRA (Loss-Informed Rank Allocation), a dynamic-rank LoRA method designed to make online rank reallocation more interpretable. LIRA scores each layer by the estimated magnitude of the local loss perturbation associated with its recent LoRA-factor movements under a second-order approximation, making the basis for each rank change interpretable term by term. By periodically applying DELTA (Displacement-Evaluated Loss-Trajectory Allocation), a displacement-based algorithm for LoRA rank reallocation, LIRA produces discrete effective ranks under matched budgets while remaining compatible with standard (A,B) adapters. candidates.title: Pretraining Data Scale Reverses the Muon-AdamW Fine-Tuning Gap
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon's advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token-parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training.

candidates.title: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Label-Efficient Facial Expression Recognition using Smart Glasses
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Facial Expression Recognition (FER) on optomyographic (OMG) smart glasses such as OCOsense enables privacy-preserving, camera-free affect sensing for health and well-being. Most FER systems are fully supervised, i.e., they rely either on hand-crafted expert features with classical machine learning, or on end-to-end deep models trained from labelled data. Both depend on large quantities of labelled expressions, which are costly to collect and limit deployment in real-world, personalized settings. We investigate Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) as a route to label-efficient FER on these glasses. We pretrain a Vision Transformer with a masked-autoencoder objective on unlabelled OCOsense recordings and finetune it for five-class FER under person-independent cross-validation. Across label budgets from 5% to 100%, pretraining consistently improves performance; with only 5% of the labels, the pretrained model outperforms the from-scratch model trained with all labels. Our results show that SSL pretraining is a practical way to reduce labelling cost for smart eyewear FER, and we discuss the implications for future personalization and continual adaptation.

candidates.abstract_excerpt: Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. candidates.title: ResQAdam: Residual-Preserving Adaptive Optimization for Memory-Efficient Quantization Aware Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.

passages.text: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .
We compare ResQAdam with AdamW in from-scratch QAT and QAT fine-tuning, in terms of training loss, final perplexity and accuracy, and optimizer-state memory.

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Table 3: Comparison of optimizer-state memory, total peak memory, and training throughput across different models. Values in each cell are formatted as AdamW / ResQAdam , with relative changes in parentheses. AdamW / ResQAdam Llama 3.2-1B Qwen2.5-1.5B Qwen3 4B-Base Opt. Total peak memory is defined as the maximum GPU memory consumed during training, encompassing weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states. All experiments utilize the Basic QAT framework with a W4A4G128 quantization configuration and a context length of 4096. Training is conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. The micro-batch size is set to 1 with 128 gradient accumulation steps. ResQAdam uses a uniform projection rank of r = 64 r=64 . The reported optimizer-state memory strictly accounts for the transformer backbone and excludes the embedding and language modeling head layers.

As detailed in Table 3 , ResQAdam consistently reduces the optimizer state footprint by over 71% across 3 different LLMs. This efficiency directly translates to a 15.3% to 19.5% reduction in total peak memory. This substantial memory reduction incurs minimal computational overhead. The training throughput decreases by less than 2% compared to standard AdamW in all evaluated cases. These results show that our amortized update strategy substantially alleviates the optimizer-state memory bottleneck of QAT while maintaining competitive training throughput.

Low-rank projection methods such as GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) and LDAdam ( Robert et al., 2024 ) restrict adaptive states to a rank- r r subspace obtained from the gradient, with LDAdam adding state transport across changing subspaces and error feedback. Structural factorization methods such as AdaFactor ( Shazeer and Stern, 2018 ) keep the full parameter dimensionality but approximate the second moment by row and column statistics. Table 4 reports the average perplexity on WikiText-2 and C4. In from-scratch QAT, every baseline is far behind ResQAdam in both quantization settings, by a margin much larger than the differences we observe between ResQAdam and AdamW in Table 1 . This is consistent with our hypothesis that confining the update to a low-rank subspace, or replacing the second moment by a factorized approximation, loses part of the correction that QAT relies on. In fine-tuning the picture depends on the bit width. At W2A16G128 the projection-based methods remain clearly behind, whereas at W4A4G128, where quantization error is small, all optimizers land within a narrow range and the choice of optimizer matters little.

passages.text: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA is governed by rank, which controls parameter budget and locally accessible task updates. Existing dynamic-rank methods mainly focus on capacity allocation, leaving unresolved whether the current adaptation space is sufficient for the task. We characterize the first-order information boundary of standard factor gradients, showing that their unobservable subspace coincides with the normal space of the low-rank manifold. Thus, factor gradients alone cannot distinguish under-optimization within the current space from task-relevant directions beyond its first-order reach. This motivates a geometric view of rank evolution, where tangent information optimizes existing degrees of freedom and the normal spectrum quantifies the value of new ones. Under a local quadratic model, we show that leading normal singular directions yield the locally optimal rank expansion, with spectral energy determining its gain. Building on this characterization, we propose GEAR, which turns the tangent–normal decomposition into rank evolution through tangent-space optimization, matrix-free normal-spectrum estimation for rank expansion, and task-induced geometric initialization. Across language and vision benchmarks, GEAR achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters. On LLaMA3-8B, it raises the average commonsense score from 86.61 to 88.45 while reducing trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.

We evaluate GEAR across commonsense reasoning, natural language understanding, and visual recognition benchmarks, considering both predictive performance and parameter efficiency. We compare against representative fixed-rank and adaptive-rank PEFT methods, including LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , AdaLoRA ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , Riemannion ( Bogachev et al., 2026 ) , GeoLoRA ( Schotthöfer et al., 2025 ) , and FlexLoRA ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . What controlled intervention isolates group-mean baseline subtraction, and how do the proposed stage-specific LoRA updates compare with standard LoRA on task quality and training cost?

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly used in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), often under similar optimizer settings. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks across multiple models show that the respective configurations for SFT and RL yield the best performance among the compared methods in most evaluated settings.

passages.section: Baseline subtraction separates the LoRA dynamics of SFT and RL (Section 2 ).
passages.text: Across various Llama and Qwen models on GSM8K [ 6 ] and MATH [ 9 ] , we observed that RL with verifiable reward via group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [ 33 ] concentrates the spectrum of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} at every learning rate; whereas SFT expands it at moderate learning rates that can facilitate desired downstream performance. For the dynamics of the singular subspaces, we observed that RL with small learning rates rotates the singular subspace much faster than SFT. Moreover, interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we find that both contrasts appear only once a group-mean baseline is subtracted from the reward, pinpointing baseline subtraction as the key mechanism that separates the LoRA dynamics of SFT and RL.

passages.section: Baseline subtraction tilts the balance between coherent fitting and gradient noise (Section 3 ).
passages.text: To understand these contrasts, we analyze a quadratic multi-index model in which a LoRA adapter is trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on pairs of correlated inputs, each pair modeling a GRPO group of responses sampled for the same prompt. Two forces compete in this model: coherent fitting that is linear in the learning rate and concentrates spectral energy on strongly responding directions, as well as feedback from gradient noise that is quadratic in the learning rate and redistributes the spectral energy more evenly. Subtracting a group-mean baseline largely cancels the gradient component shared across a group’s responses, which drives coherent fitting along pretrained directions and anchors successive updates to similar directions, while retaining most of the component that contrasts responses within the group, and damping the gradient noise from task-irrelevant directions. Coherent fitting thus persists through the contrasts while the redistributing feedback loses relative strength, and gradient noise, no longer anchored by the shared component, steers the update directions more, leading to spectral concentration and faster singular subspace rotation during RL. Nevertheless, baseline subtraction can come at a cost for prediction: coherent fitting of the shared component reduces the risk more efficiently than fitting of the contrasts, cancellation of which shrinks the risk reduction from coherent fitting (linear in the learning rate) relative to the cost of gradient noise (quadratic in the learning rate). The risk-favorable learning rate thus remains low, consistent with the common practice in RL.

passages.section: The dynamics inform stage-specific LoRA optimization (Section 4 ).
passages.text: Our analysis further shows which dynamics accompany the risk-favorable learning rate: training without a baseline (as in SFT) expands the spectrum of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} , whereas training with a baseline (as in RL) concentrates the spectrum and rotates the left singular subspace faster. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor the update of LoRA factors to each stage by combining two standard components, a norm-preserving spectral flattening as in Muon [ 14 ] and a per-factor choice between SGD and Adam update directions. In SFT, we flatten the singular spectrum of the full update of the factor so that the adaptation is distributed more evenly across singular directions; whereas in RL, we flatten only the component of the update orthogonal to the current left singular subspace of Δ ​ W t \Delta W_{t} , which promotes subspace rotation while leaving the within-subspace component unchanged. The resulting configurations achieve dominating downstream performance across most evaluated models and tasks.

Rotation measures how much the span of the adapter’s columns changes between checkpoints. Shared responses repeatedly pull updates toward similar directions, helping to stabilize this span across sampled groups. Baseline subtraction suppresses these responses more strongly than within-group contrasts, as reflected by ϑ a < ϑ o \vartheta_{a}<\vartheta_{o} . Differences between sampled groups consequently have greater influence on the directions of subsequent updates. Then the span changes more between records, giving smaller left singular-subspace overlap. For risk, the leading prediction gain is linear in the learning rate, while gradient noise contributes a quadratic cost. In this model, fitting the task component along pretrained directions gives more prediction progress per unit residual energy. Since ϑ a < ϑ o \vartheta_{a}<\vartheta_{o} , baseline subtraction suppresses this shared component more strongly, reducing useful progress relative to the noise cost. The favorable learning-rate range therefore shifts downward, yielding the opposite rate preferences in the theorem.

In this work, we identify distinct spectral and subspace dynamics of LoRA under SFT and RL. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. However, it remains unclear whether Muon’s advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token–parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training. The Muon optimizer has recently shown strong empirical performance for pretraining LLMs, challenging AdamW’s status as the standard optimizer for minimizing pretraining loss ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) . Prior work has shown that the pretraining optimization choices that minimize pretraining loss do not necessarily yield the best model after fine-tuning ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . What ultimately matters downstream is the learning–forgetting tradeoff : how well a fine-tuned model learns the target task while retaining its pretrained knowledge. Motivated by this, we ask: Does Muon’s pretraining advantage over AdamW extend to the learning–forgetting tradeoff? To answer this question, we measure the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap , which compares the two optimizers on this tradeoff; a negative gap indicates that the Muon pretrained model dominates the AdamW pretrained model after fine-tuning, and a positive gap indicates the reverse. We show that the answer depends on the pretraining data budget, and find that pretraining data scale reverses the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap . At small budgets, Muon achieves lower fine-tuning loss with less forgetting than AdamW and the fine-tuning gap is negative. At larger budgets, this trend reverses: AdamW achieves a better learning–forgetting tradeoff than Muon, and the fine-tuning gap becomes positive.

In Section 3 , we pretrain OLMo-style 30M–600M models ( Groeneveld et al., 2024 ; Team OLMo et al., 2025 ) on 150 150 M to 154 154 B DCLM tokens ( Li et al., 2024 ) , comparing AdamW and Muon, and fine-tune each base model on four datasets while sweeping the fine-tuning optimizer and learning rate, for nearly 600 pretraining runs and 29,000 fine-tuning runs in total. We show that when tuning pretraining hyperparameters for the lowest pretraining loss, Muon consistently achieves lower loss than AdamW. However, with sufficient pretraining data, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning, reversing the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap. This reversal also holds when we disregard pretraining loss, instead sweeping pretraining hyperparameters to obtain the best learning–forgetting tradeoff after fine-tuning. We additionally show that as model size scales, AdamW surpasses Muon at progressively smaller data budgets . In Section 4 , we investigate why the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap reverses as the pretraining data budget grows. Fine-tuning changes the output distribution, so we generalize fine-tuning updates with perturbations to the output distribution and study which optimizer produces base models that are more robust to such perturbations. To quantify sensitivity to output perturbations, we introduce the margin-to-spread ratio (MSR) , a simple metric derived from the model’s output logits that characterizes robustness. For each prediction, the MSR is the difference between the correct logit and the average of the incorrect logits, normalized by the spread of the incorrect logits ( Section 4.1 ): a prediction is more robust when the MSR is larger.

We test whether the budget trend predicted by Section 4.2 also appears in real language models, beyond the assumptions used in our theoretical analysis. Setup. We evaluate the AdamW and Muon models trained in Section 3 , spanning five model sizes, on held-out DCLM text. We compute the MSR at each token position and report the median over correctly predicted positions. At each position, h h and κ \kappa are the mean and standard deviation of the margins between the correct next-token logit and all other vocabulary logits. We use the median to reduce sensitivity to outliers; Section 4.1 instead uses the mean margin divided by the square root of the mean variance. Experimental Result. Figure 5 plots the MSR for the three model sizes with the widest budget ranges, from 30M to 100M. Muon has a larger MSR at small data budgets, while AdamW has a larger MSR at sufficiently large budgets. As the budget grows, the difference between AdamW’s and Muon’s MSRs increases, and the ratio of AdamW’s MSR to Muon’s crosses one. This shift toward AdamW is consistent with the theoretical budget trend and parallels the reversal in relative robustness to fine-tuning observed in Section 3 . Are there experiments on neural-network or language-model training beyond the theoretical example, and what limitations does the paper state?

passages.text: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton–Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton–Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton–Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four. † † shortheadings: Finite-Depth Newton–Schulz Dynamics / Long † † firstpage: 1 † † heading: 2026 1–

We consider a two-layer neural network with quadratic activation and all second-layer weights fixed to one. This model admits an equivalent representation as a positive-semidefinite matrix factorization. Such quadratic networks provide a tractable setting for analyzing nonlinear training dynamics, and have also been studied through gradient flow and spectral gradient methods ( Martin et al., 2024 ; Martin et al., 2026 ; Braun et al., 2026 ) . We study continuous-time optimization dynamics in which K K cubic Newton–Schulz iterations are applied to the normalized factor gradient, and refer to K K as the spectral depth. For the analysis, we use a two-scale Gaussian initialization: one hidden row is initialized at scale ε \varepsilon , while the remaining rows have scale ε b \varepsilon^{b} , where b > 1 b>1 . The gradient normalization includes an additive stabilization proportional to ε \varepsilon . This choice of initialization scales allows us to identify the leading directional dynamics first and then derive the coupled equations governing the weaker components in the remaining independent directions. We compare trajectories on the same task and with the same underlying Gaussian seed as ε \varepsilon tends to zero, while keeping each spectral depth fixed. Removing the row-dependent initialization scales would instead lead to an isotropic Gaussian initialization, for which the competing directions may exhibit different and potentially richer dynamics. The analysis of this regime remains open.

Another question concerns the extent to which small-initialization asymptotics can determine the subsequent training trajectory. Under suitable structural conditions, gradient flow admits a precise description in which the initialization scale can be used to reverse-engineer the full training dynamics, leading also to a characterization of time-dependent implicit regularization ( Berthier, 2023 ) . For finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics, the nonlinear matrix iteration prevents this reconstruction argument from carrying over directly. Although the dynamics can be analyzed in a small neighborhood of the origin, the resulting local description does not by itself determine the trajectory after leaving that neighborhood. This creates two distinct dynamical scales: the entrance dynamics near the origin and the subsequent evolution away from it. Establishing how the entrance dynamics are transmitted to the later trajectory is one of the main results of this paper.

Following the framework of Li et al. (2021) , which characterizes the first nonzero stationary point selected by gradient flow under suitable assumptions, we study the evolution from small initialization through the first stationary point encountered after escape. This allows us to compare the stationary points approached by gradient descent and by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics. Under an additional structural assumption, we establish a sufficient large-depth guarantee: for all sufficiently large spectral depths, the selected Newton–Schulz continuation approaches a first stationary point whose loss is strictly smaller than that of the first stationary point selected by gradient descent. For smaller depths, our results do not provide a general criterion determining whether the trajectory visits or bypasses the gradient-descent stationary point. Moreover, without the additional assumption, the first stationary points reached by finite-depth Newton–Schulz dynamics and gradient descent may have the same loss. Such equal-loss behavior may reveal further dynamical structures, which we leave for future work. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model and pathwise comparison criteria. Sections 3–5 establish the Gaussian entrance law, continuation criteria, and eventual depth guarantee. Section 6 presents an exact empirical task, and Section 7 discusses the scope of the results and open questions. Detailed proofs are given in the appendices.

In this paper, we have studied how finitely many iterations of a nonlinear matrix transformation can reshape optimization dynamics. In a quadratic two-layer network, we have characterized the evolution from small-initialization escape near the origin to the first nonzero stationary stage. Our results provide a precise description of how the number of Newton–Schulz iterations controls early rank selection and regulates the subsequent optimization path. Beyond this particular model, the analysis offers a framework combining spectral dynamics with small-initialization techniques, which may help understand certain training phenomena arising in large-scale neural networks, including language models. Of particular interest are networks with nonlinear activations such as ReLU, high-dimensional training regimes, and deeper architectures, where the interaction between spectral updates and feature learning may lead to richer dynamics.

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

passages.text: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates descent directions from function values alone, which removes the activation storage required by backpropagation and makes it attractive for memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). Existing low-rank ZO methods either parameterize the additive update through Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation, or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank. In this work, we propose to constrain each additive update block to a fixed-rank matrix manifold while keeping the pretrained weights frozen, so the learned update remains rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning. On this geometry, we build a Riemannian ZO gradient estimator that projects a random matrix onto the tangent space, normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch induced by projection, and further propose Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S. We show that the ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation, and ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. Experiments on LLM fine-tuning tasks show that the proposed algorithms are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of domains ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ) . Fine-tuning these models on downstream tasks is crucial for their practical deployment. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) have emerged as a practical solution, training low-rank updates while keeping pretrained weights frozen ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Hayou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024a ) . However, first-order optimization still incurs substantial memory overhead from storing activations for backpropagation, especially in long-context settings where activations dominate memory. To enhance memory efficiency, zeroth-order (ZO) fine-tuning methods ( Malladi et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) estimate descent directions from function values without backpropagated gradients, avoiding the activation storage required by backward passes ( Spall, 1992 ) .

Recent low-rank ZO fine-tuning methods combine these two directions by restricting the finite-difference search through low-rank perturbations, adapter factors, gradient estimators, or random subspaces ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Song and Li, 2026 ) . Factor-based approaches constrain the learned update through adapter coordinates, whereas low-rank perturbation methods constrain individual ZO steps. These two branches of methods differ in the way of constructing low-rank additive update matrices when optimizing a fixed-rank update matrix. Factor-based adaptation uses a factorized update Δ ​ 𝑾 = 𝑩 ​ 𝑨 \Delta\boldsymbol{W}=\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{A} and optimizes over ( 𝑩 , 𝑨 ) (\boldsymbol{B},\boldsymbol{A}) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . This representation is nonunique, since ( 𝑩 ​ 𝑸 ) ​ ( 𝑸 − 1 ​ 𝑨 ) (\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{Q})(\boldsymbol{Q}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}) gives the same update for any invertible 𝑸 \boldsymbol{Q} . Low-rank perturbation and random-subspace methods instead use restricted finite-difference directions or estimators to construct each ZO step ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024b ) . FP4Quant integrates a micro-grouped dual-scale FP4 quantization mechanism to preserve local tensor distribution characteristics, a warp-cooperative FP4 packing scheme to enable efficient sub-byte data representation, and a hybrid two-level FWHT pipeline to mitigate quantization errors with GPU-aware execution optimization. Experiments on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with Qwen-7B demonstrate up to 1.56 × \times end-to-end throughput improvement over BF16, revealing a trade-off between throughput and model quality.

The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has made communication overhead a critical bottleneck in distributed model-parallel training. Although existing low-precision compression methods can effectively reduce communication costs, further reducing the communication footprint to ultra-low-bit formats such as FP4 introduces new challenges, including limited numerical range, sub-byte storage overhead, and increased computational cost from fine-grained quantization. In this paper, we present FP4Quant , a micro-grouped FP4 compression framework for efficient model-parallel LLM training. FP4Quant integrates a micro-grouped dual-scale FP4 quantization mechanism to preserve local tensor distribution characteristics, a warp-cooperative FP4 packing scheme to enable efficient sub-byte data representation, and a hybrid two-level FWHT pipeline to mitigate quantization errors with GPU-aware execution optimization. Experiments on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with Qwen-7B demonstrate up to 1.56 × \times end-to-end throughput improvement over BF16, revealing a trade-off between throughput and model quality.
